bssd

bssd computes the posterior probability of a safety signal from blinded clinical trial data with the models examined by Duncan (2026). The posterior quantities are obtained by numerical integration instead of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, so the results do not depend on a random seed and are fast enough for simulation studies.

Models and functions

Model Data Function Relative risk
BDRIBS(1) number of subjects with the event and total exposure time bdribs_post() rate ratio
BDRIBS(2) number of subjects with the event and total time at risk bdribs_post() rate ratio
EXP_BERN event indicator and follow-up time of each subject expbern_post() rate ratio
LL_BERN event indicator and follow-up time of each subject llbern_post() ratio of the cumulative incidences at t_star

BDRIBS is the Poisson-based model of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018). With pt_hp = Inf, bdribs_post() performs their screening analysis with a known background rate. The results of the three functions have print() and summary() methods.

Other functions:

  • time_at_risk(): total exposure time and total time at risk from subject-level data.
  • ll_cdf() and ll_mu(): cumulative incidence and location parameter of the log-logistic distribution.
  • sim_blinded(): simulation of blinded trial data.
  • sim_oc(): operating characteristics of the models by simulation.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("gosukehommaEX/bssd")

Examples

Hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Section 4.4) has 9 subjects with the event in 540 patient-years of blinded exposure, a 2:1 randomization, and a known background rate of 0.011 per patient-year on placebo.

library(bssd)
fit <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                   pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit
#> Model: BDRIBS 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.753
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.522, median 1.438, 95% interval (0.379, 3.143)

The posterior probability of r > 1 is 0.753. The article reports 0.756, computed by MCMC with the bdribs package.

The four models applied to simulated subject-level data (150 subjects, 1:1 randomization, log-logistic times to the event, analysis at week 117):

set.seed(2026)
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(5.85, 0.8))
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
lambda_hp <- -log(1 - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8)) / 104
pt_weeks <- 75 * 104
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks,
                        df = 2),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2),
  EXP_BERN = expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                          lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2),
  LL_BERN = llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                        sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = pt_weeks / 52, df_p = 2,
                        t_star = 104)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "error")]
#>             model      prob signal rr_median        error
#> BDRIBS1   BDRIBS1 0.7909268  FALSE  2.879204           NA
#> BDRIBS2   BDRIBS2 0.8049487  FALSE  3.030938           NA
#> EXP_BERN EXP_BERN 0.8202780  FALSE  3.242503 1.814905e-07
#> LL_BERN   LL_BERN 0.9351465  FALSE  4.217216 3.733315e-04

vignette("bssd") explains the models, the priors of this example and the simulation of the operating characteristics. The documentation is also available at https://gosukehommaex.github.io/bssd/.

Validation

  • tests/testthat has 24 test files with 48 test_that() blocks. Their expected values were computed beforehand by independent Python implementations (inst/validation/python).
  • inst/reproduce reproduces the numerical results of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) and Duncan (2026): tables, worked examples and simulations.
  • inst/validation compares bdribs_post() with the bdribs package, expbern_post() and llbern_post() with MCMC in JAGS, the default integration grids with finer grids and with an independent Python implementation, and sim_oc() with an independent Python simulation.

Each item is judged as PASS (agreement within the tolerance), EXPLAINED (a difference whose reason is registered), FAIL (a difference without a registered reason) or INFO (no value to compare with):

file PASS EXPLAINED FAIL INFO
reproduce_Duncan2026.csv 15 6 0 7
reproduce_Duncan2026_prior.csv 23 6 0 0
reproduce_Duncan2026_simulation.csv 14 4 0 113
reproduce_Mukhopadhyay2018.csv 82 4 0 1
validate_bdribs_package.csv 35 0 0 0
validate_convergence.csv 19 0 0 0
validate_jags.csv 24 0 0 3
validate_sim_oc.csv 29 0 0 0

The reasons for the EXPLAINED items are listed in inst/reproduce/results/SUMMARY.md.

References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 36(2), 227-244. https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 17(6), 823-834. https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898
